headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and capability conflict; Goose’s filesystem/MCP/tooling can ingest EMQX outputs and act on them.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose can read files, use MCP, and process stdin/stdout, while EMQX exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress. If EMQX outputs attacker-controlled content into a shared workspace or MCP-fed channel, Goose may treat it as instructions. The pair has a plausible bridge, but no direct documented injection path is shown.
conditions: IF EMQX output is written into a shared file or MCP resource that Goose reads
IF Goose parses EMQX-generated text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of EMQX outputs into Goose prompts
Require provenance tags on any EMQX-produced file before Goose reads it
Route EMQX output to a read-only log instead of a shared workspace
Add a manual review step before Goose acts on EMQX text
requires-engineering: isolate the agents into separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Goose reads and writes the user filesystem and handles model-provider and extension tokens. A shared workspace can expose EMQX data to Goose, and Goose may transmit that context to configured providers. This is a plausible default-path leakage risk, though not directly evidenced beyond the profiles.
conditions: IF EMQX stores IoT data in a directory Goose can read
IF Goose forwards that directory contents to a configured model provider or extension
mitigations: Move EMQX data outside Goose-readable paths
Restrict Goose to a dedicated least-privilege workspace
Redact sensitive IoT fields before Goose processes files
Rotate any extension tokens exposed in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem ACL separation between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shells, and spawn subprocesses; EMQX can emit networked outputs but has no write controls shown. The main conflict is with Goose’s shared-state model via filesystem: concurrent instances can overwrite each other, and if EMQX artifacts are stored in the same tree, Goose can mutate them. Uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF Goose instances share the same filesystem tree
IF Goose modifies git state or files that EMQX also reads or writes
mitigations: Use separate working directories per agent
Pause one Goose instance before the other writes shared files
Avoid running Goose on repositories EMQX depends on
Commit or snapshot state before Goose edits it
requires-engineering: add locking around shared filesystem paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can act on files, shell commands, and MCP tools, so EMQX-produced outputs could become inputs to downstream actions if treated as authoritative. EMQX itself is an IoT broker/API surface, not a verifier. The pair therefore supports a classic unverified-output cascade, but the profiles do not show fully autonomous destructive actions by default.
conditions: IF Goose consumes EMQX output as a source of truth
IF Goose then executes shell, MCP, or file-write actions based on that output
mitigations: Require Goose to verify EMQX-derived facts against a second source
Insert a human approval gate before any Goose action
Mark EMQX output as untrusted in prompts and templates
Limit Goose to read-only analysis for EMQX-derived artifacts
requires-engineering: add schema validation for EMQX outputs

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Goose handles source code, files in cwd, and extension/model-provider tokens. No explicit residency or certification mismatch is documented for either profile, so only a limited compliance-gap risk is visible. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling of sensitive data classes, but the profiles do not prove a specific regulatory breach.
conditions: IF IoT data subject to a stricter policy is placed into Goose-managed files
IF Goose sends those files to a provider or extension outside the required jurisdiction
mitigations: Keep regulated IoT data out of Goose workspaces
Document the data classes allowed in Goose sessions
Disable extensions that export files off-host
Review retention settings for both tools
requires-engineering: map data flows to residency and retention controls
